blocks.html:
Ejection fraction (EF): the proportion of blood that is ejected from the ventricles; a continuum measured with echocardiogram,

nuclear medicine scans, or cardiac catheterization

  • EF = SV/EDV, where SV = EDV – ESV
  • Normal = 50-60%
  • Moderately impaired = 30-35%
  • Severely decreased < 25%
  • Heart failure: heart wall muscle slowly weakens and loses its ability to pump blood
  • Patients with systolic heart failure have a reduced EF
  • Patients may have heart failure with a normal EF – diastolic failure, heart failure

with normal/preserved EF (HFpEF)

-Children and young adults may have a normal S3

  • S4 = atrial filling phase of diastole

Aortic Pressures
  • Systolic pressure: maximum aortic pressure during contraction
  • Dicrotic notch: dip that separates systolic and diastolic parts of the aortic pressure waveform; closure of the aortic valve
  • Diastolic pressure: minimum aortic pressure during diastole
  • Mean arterial pressure (MAP): average BP during a single cardiac cycle; provided by NIBP cuff or invasive arterial monitoring

MAP = DP + 1/3(SP – DP) = 93 mmHg

MAP = CO × TPR
•Pulse pressure = systolic BP – diastolic BP

Clinical Questions
•
Can you think of an example where the output of the right and left ventricle would NOT be matched? Septal defectà hole in the heart causes a mismatch
•
LVEDV is 100 mL and stroke volume is 50 mL – what is the ejection fraction? EF = SV/EDV = 50/100 = 50% (normal)
•
LVEDV is 200 mL and SV is 50 mL. EF is 25%;LVESV is 150 mL à SV is normal, CO is maintained; systolic heart failure
•
LEDV is 100 mL and SV is 25. EF is 25% àlow SV, low CO
•
A patient has decreased capillary refill. Possible reasons include:
They are cold – vasoconstriction
o
They are hypovolemic – compensatory response to maintain BP and perfusion
o
Their cardiac output is low – decreased perfusion to nonvital organs
o
Septic patients will be vasodilated and have a normal capillary refill, but “cold sepsis” can decrease CO and cause relative hypovolemia
o
•
What is the pressure in the capillaries (approximately)? 20 mm Hg à above this gives pulmonary edema
•
What happens if the pressures in the surrounding tissues exceeds this? Decreased perfusion at the cellular level à capillaries get squished
Intracranial hypertensionà brain damage and ultimately brain death; high ICP > 20 mm Hg
o
Intraabdominal hypertensionà decreased kidney perfusion, bowel ischemia, respiratory failure, and cardiovascular collapse (abdominal
o
compartment syndrome – treated with abdominal decompression); high IAP > 20 mm Hg
Compartment syndrome of an extremityà fasciotomy surgery to relieve swelling and pressure
o
Endotracheal tube cuffà high pressure within the cuff can affect flow to the tracheal mucosa; can cause necrosis and lead to tracheal stenosis
o
•
Sometimes a balloon device is inserted into the esophagus if there is bleeding from dilated esophageal veins (esophageal varices). If the esophageal balloon
is inflated – what pressure should it be inflated to? 20 mm Hg (enough to stop the bleeding, but is safe against esophageal necrosis and ischemia)
•
Ophthalmologists measure the pressure in your eye (intra- ocular pressure) to diagnose glaucoma. What would be considered a high IOP? > 20 mm Hg
•
If the left heart fails and there are higher LV diastolic pressures could this affect the right heart? Yesà LA pressure will be high; RV will have to generate
higher pressures to move blood forward from R to L across the pulmonary circulation
•
The most common cause of right heart failure is: Left heart failure

Cardiac Electrical Physiology

Action potential: a rapid change in electrical balance across a physiological membrane

  • Resting stage: membrane is polarized
  • Depolarization: membrane potential moves towards zero

Threshold potential: voltage at which an AP is triggered

  • o V.G. Na+ channels open, Na+ flows into the cell
  • Repolarization: return of the membrane potential to its resting value

V.G. K+ channels begin opening, K+ flows out of the cell

  • o V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated
  • Hyperpolarization: membrane potential moves to more negative values

K+ continues to leave the cell as V.G. K+ channels close slowly

  • Absolute refractory period: another AP cannot be generated
  • Relative refractory period: a stronger than normal stimulus is required to

generate an AP; some V.G. Na+ channels have recovered

  • Local anesthetics (lidocaine, procaine) function through their ability to block APs

in nerve fibres responsible for pain

Act directly on V.G. Na+ channels, making them more difficult to open

  • o Membrane potential: due to an imbalance of charged ions inside and outside cell

membranes – gradient for ions to diffuse down

  • To determine how an ion affects electrical potential across membranes, consider:

The charge of each ion

  • o The permeability of the membrane to that ion
  • o The relative concentration of the ion on each side of the membrane
  • K+: high intracellular concentration (140 mEq/L), low extracellular concentration (4 mEq/L)
  • Na+: low intracellular concentration (14 mEq/L), high extracellular concentration (140 mEq/L)
  • This balance is maintained by the Na+/K+ exchange pump and “leak” channels that allow ions to travel down their concentration

gradients (far more permeable to K+ than Na+) – resting membrane potential = -90 mV

blocks.html:
Clinical Relevance
  • The phases of cardiac cell depolarization are influenced greatly by the concentration and balance of ions on either side of the cell membrane;

derangements in this balance can lead to heart failure and life-threatening arrhythmias

  • Always exercise caution when administering solutions containing ions to patients
  • NEVER rapidly administer a K+ bolus, as this will almost certainly result in cardiac arrest and lead to death
Rhythmicity
  • The heart has a system that is able to generate rhythmical electrical impulses
  • The fibers of the SA node have the capacity of self-excitation

RMP = -55 mV to -60 mV

  • o Leak of Na+ and Ca2+ into the cell of the SA node is greater as compared to other cells (skeletal or cardiac muscle),
  • o which leads to a gradual rise of intracellular membrane potential (less negative)
  • Threshold potential = -40 mVà V.G. Na+ channels open, AP initiated
  • o Repolarization: V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated, V.G. K+ channels open
  • Other parts of the conduction system also have potential for spontaneous depolarization, but they have a slower intrinsic rate

than the SA node

AV node may take over as the pacemaker if the SA node is not working

  • o If these are insufficient or also fail, then cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest may occur, which would require an
  • o emergent artificial pacemaker – applied to the chest wall or via a wire that enters the RV

Electrocardiogram Basics

Electrocardiogram (ECG, EKG): records the electrical activity of the heart – myocardial contraction

  • AS A WAVE OF POSITIVE CHARGES OF DEPOLARIZATION WITHIN THE MYOCYTES FLOWS TOWARD A POSITIVE ELECTRODE,

THERE IS A POSITIVE (UPWARD) DEFLECTION RECORDED ON THE ECG

  • Most of the ECG QRS reflects the LV because of its high mass – current flows from top to bottom, then R to L

blocks.alt: Figure from the Electrocardiogram Basics and ECG Interpretation notes

blocks.html:
• ECG is recorded on graph paper
  • Smallest divisions = 1 × 1 mm
  • Heavy black squares = 5 × 5 mm
  • Horizontal axis = time (1 mm = 40 ms, 5 mm = 200 ms)
  • Vertical axis = amplitude/voltage (10 mm = 1 mV)
  • Calibration signal = 1 box wide × 2 boxes high
  • Lead changeover marker = small spike

blocks.html:
ECG Waves

  • P wave: atrial depolarization and contraction
  • PR interval: pause at AV node before ventricular depolarization; 120-200 ms
  • QRS complex: ventricular depolarization and contraction; 80-120 ms
  • Q wave: first downward deflection of the complex; often absent
  • R wave: first upward deflection of the complex
  • S wave: any downward wave preceded by an upward wave
  • QS wave: no upward wave
  • ST segment: plateau phase of ventricular repolarization

-Normally level with baseline – pathology if elevated or depressed

  • T wave: late phase of rapid ventricular repolarization
  • QT interval: duration of ventricular systole

-Normal = less than half of the R-to-R interval at normal rates

-Males≤ 440 ms; females ≤ 460 ms

-Elongation: genetics, drugs, electrolytes, hypothermia

  • U wave: ventricular repolarization; can be normal or a sign of hypokalemia

  • Say “300, 150, 100” … “75, 60, 50”
  • Calculate: rate = cycles/10 second strip × 6
  • Sinus bradycardia: rate < 60/min
  • Sinus tachycardia: rate > 100/min
Rhythm
  • Identify the basic rhythm, then scan tracing for prematurity, pauses, irregularity, and abnormal waves
  • Check for: P before each QRS, QRS after each P, PR intervals (for AV blocks), QRS interval (for BBB)
  • If axis deviation, rule out hemiblock
Axis
  • Normal = -30° to +90°; check lead I and AVF; check lead II for left axis
  • QRS above or below baseline for axis quadrant
  • For axis in degrees, find isoelectric QRS in a limb lead of axis quadrant – use “Axis in Degrees” chart
  • Axis rotation in the horizontal plane – find translational QRS

Ischemia and Infarction
  • Check for: Q waves (necrosis/past infarction), inverted T waves (ischemia), ST elevation (infarction), ST depression (ischemia)
  • Reciprocal changes: ST elevation ± ST depression on the mirror side of the STEMI location = true STEMI

STEMI locations: big LII, little LI, ASS, ALL

  • o The boot: elevation in II, III, AVF (inferior STEMI) patients (with RVI) vitals are typically in their boots
  • o Widow maker: elevation in V1-V4; affects the entire LAD artery
  • Find the location of the pathology, then identify the occluded coronary artery

blocks.html:
Contractility (inotropy): the intrinsic property of cardiac muscle cells to shorten in

response to a stimulus (action potential)

  • Independent of preload and afterload – based on the intrinsic strength of

contraction of heart muscle

  • Shortening of cardiac muscle tissue results in ejection of blood
  • Increased with sympathetic nervous system activation
  • Increase in contractility will increase SV for any given preload
  • Systolic heart failure: downward/right shift and flattening of the curve; will not

respond properly to volume

Fluid to increase preload – may increase SV and CO, but may also

  • o increase end-diastolic pressure and cause pulmonary edema

Decrease afterload – only if a patient is hypertensive

  • o Increase contractility – does not improve long-term mortality
  • o Module Questions
  • 8. The most common cause of right heart failure is: Left heart failureà pulmonary embolism, chronic lung disease, idiopathic pulmonary hypertension, and

chronic hypoxemia due to altitude may also cause right heart failure

  • 9. You are examining a patient and note that the jugular venous pressure is elevated to the angle of their jaw. This may be caused by: All of the aboveà

volume overload, right heart failure, and tricuspid regurgitation will tend to have an increase in right atrial pressure and JVP; cardiac tamponade is

pressure in the pericardium surrounding the heart that impairs venous return and CO

10.A noncompliant (stiff) ventricle may be associated with all of the following (aortic stenosis, chronic hypertension, mitral stenosis, acute cardiac ischemia,

  • heart failure with preserved ejection fraction) EXCEPT: Mitral stenosisà will cause an increase in left atrial pressures and a pressure gradient across the

mitral valve; the LV is not affected directly, the problem is ventricular filling from the atrium to the ventricle

11.Typically, atrial contraction contributes a relatively small amount to diastolic filling; however, some patients will have a disproportionate decrease in

  • cardiac output if they develop atrial fibrillation. Examples where this is the case include: All of the aboveà anything that contributes to a stiff

noncompliant ventricle will increase the importance of atrial systole to ventricular filling in diastole and CO (aortic stenosis, stiff noncompliant ventricle,

hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); if the mitral valve is stenotic, it will not open easily, and atrial contraction will provide an extra “kick” for ventricular filling

12.A patient acutely develops a large pulmonary embolism and becomes hemodynamically unstable with tachycardia, hypotension, and signs of decreased

  • perfusion (low urine output and decreased capillary refill). An echocardiogram is MOST likely to show: Dilated right ventricleà an acute PE is an abrupt

increase in RV afterload; if the RV is unable to handle this it will fail and acutely dilate; the LV will not be directly affected, but may be indirectly affected if

the RV dilates and pushes the interventricular septum over toward the LV

  • 13.Chronic mitral regurgitation would most likely be associated with: All of the aboveà with mitral regurgitation, there will be blood flowing back into the LA

during ventricular systole and this will be reflected back into the pulmonary vasculature; LA enlargement, LV enlargement because it has volume overload,

tendency to pulmonary edema, eccentric hypertrophy

14.Compliance is defined as the relationship between: Pressure and volume

blocks.html:
Nerves of the Mediastinum

  • R/L phrenic nerves: arise in neck from spinal nerves C3-C5 to

innervate the diaphragm; often embedded in fat around the

pericardial sac

  • R/L vagus nerves: descend from the neck into the superior

mediastinum; found posterior to the root of the lung, which

helps distinguish them from the phrenic nerves

  • L recurrent laryngeal nerve: branch of the L vagus nerve that

supplies many muscles of the larynx; loops under the arch of

the aorta and ascends between the trachea and esophagus to

return to the larynx

  • R recurrent laryngeal nerve: loops around the R subclavian

artery and ascends between the trachea and esophagus to the

larynx; it is NOT located in the superior mediastinum

  • Sympathetic chain: bilateral trunks of the sympathetic nervous

system situated on either side of the vertebral column from the

base of the skull to the coccyx;

-There are typically 12 ganglia (postsynaptic cell bodies) in the

thoracic portion of each sympathetic trunk

-Most presynaptic sympathetic fibres synapse in ganglia along

the sympathetic trunk

  • Thoracic splanchnic nerves: presynaptic nerves that travel

through the sympathetic trunk in the thorax without synapsing;

continue through the diaphragm and into the abdomen to

provide sympathetic innervation to abdominal organs

  • Greater splanchnic nerves: arise from branches of the

sympathetic chain at the level of the 5th-9th ganglia

  • Lesser splanchnic nerves: arise from the 10th and 11th ganglia
  • Least splanchnic nerves: arise from the 12th thoracic ganglion

Other Structures in the Mediastinum

  • Trachea: extends from the larynx to the superior

mediastinum, anterior to the esophagus; ends with the

carina at the level of the sternal angle where it bifurcates

into the right and left primary bronchi; it is NOT part of the

posterior mediastinum

  • Ligamentum arteriosum: remnant of fetal ductus arteriosum

that served to shunt blood from the pulmonary trunk to the

inferior surface of the aortic arch

  • Esophagus:extends from the pharynx and passes posterior to

the trachea; runs the entire length of the thorax before piercing

the diaphragm to enter the stomach

  • Thoracic duct: main lymphatic duct of the body; begins in the

abdomen and enters the thorax to the R of the aorta; ascends

to the base of the neck to drain into the venous system at the

junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins

Pericardial sac: protective, fluid filled, triple-layered sac that surrounds the heart and roots of the great vessels

  • Fibrous pericardium(outer layer): dense, inelastic, connective tissue that attaches to the diaphragm to anchor the heart;

provides protection for the heart and prevents it from overstretching

  • Serous pericardium: thin, double-layered membrane around the heart that secretes serous fluid

1.Parietal pericardium: lines the internal aspect of the fibrous pericardium

Pericardial cavity: contains serous fluid to reduce friction between the membranes as the heart moves

  • o 2.Visceral pericardium: lines the heart and roots of the great vessels

• Sensory innervation: phrenic nerve (C3-C5) – pain radiates to the ipsilateral supraclavicular

region (top of the shoulder)

  • Sympathetic innervation: cardiopulmonary splanchnic nerves (T1-T4)
  • Parasympathetic innervation: vagus nerve
Clinical Note
  • Pericarditis: painful inflammation of the pericardium that causes the surface of the pericardium to become

rough, creating friction, which can be heard as a rustling sound with a stethoscope

  • Pericardial effusion: passage of fluid into the pericardial cavity
  • Cardiac tamponade: compression of the heart that is a potentially lethal condition

Can occur from cardiomegaly (enlarged heart), or an illness/wound that causes blood or fluid to

  • o enter the pericardium

If extensive effusion exists, the compromised volume of the sac does not allow full expansion of the

  • o heart; this will limit the amount of blood the heart can receive and reduces CO as a result

Pericardiocentesis is used to remove fluid from the pericardium to relieve pressure by inserting a

  • o wide-bore needle into the 5th or 6th intercostal space near the sternum or via the infrasternal angle
Anatomy of the Heart
  • Located in the inferior, middle mediastinum; rests on the diaphragm between the lungs and the ribs
  • The apex of the heart lies on the left side of the body
  • Generates and conducts electrical impulses for contraction so blood can be transported to the lungs and throughout the body

rows:
•R auricle and anterior portion contain pectinate muscles
•Crista terminalis separates pectinate muscles (muscular ridges)
from the smooth posterior wall
•Fossa ovalis: the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale that
allowed blood to be shunted to the L side of the heart
Three veins deliver blood to the RA:
•SVC: venous return from upper body
•IVC: venous return from the lower body (largest vein)
•Coronary sinus: venous return from heart tissue – enters the RA
between the right AV valve and the opening of the IVC

• Bases of the tricuspid valve are attached to a fibrous ring that
resists dilation; the free edges of the valve cusps are attached to
chordae tendineae(cords of tendons)
•Papillary muscles anchor the tricuspid valve
•Septomarginal trabecula contains part of the conducting system
of the heart, which facilitates coordinated contraction of the RV
• When the ventricle contracts, the chordae tendineae and
papillary muscles prevent the valve cusps from being pushed back
into the atrium by the force of the contraction
•Trabeculae carneae: muscular ridges similar to the RA
• Blood is pumped from the conus arteriosus of the R, smooth
portion just inferior to the pulmonary semilunar valve, into the
pulmonary trunk that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs

• Has a smooth interior with walls slightly thicker than the RA
• Forms most of the base of the heart
•L auricle is small and contains pectinate muscleswhile the rest of
the LA is smooth walled
Four pulmonary veins deliver oxygenated blood to the LA:
• R superior vein
• L superior vein
• R inferior vein
• L inferior vein

•Mitral valve has chordae tendineae attached to two large
papillary musclesthat are attached to the walls of the LV
• The papillary muscles contract as the LV contracts
• LV is larger and has thicker walls then the RV because the LV
pumps systemically and thus is under greater pressure
• LV contains numerous, small trabeculae carneae
• Oxygenated blood is pumped systemically from the LV through an
aortic semilunar valve into the ascending aorta, which has left,
right, and posterior cusps

Coronary circulation
  • The heart has its own circulation to supply cardiac tissue – heart is fed with oxygenated blood first
  • The first two branches from the ascending aorta at the aortic sinuses are the R and L coronary arteries
  • R coronary artery: runs within the coronary sulcus

SA nodal artery – ascends to SA node to supply the pulmonary trunk and SA node

  • o R marginal artery – passes to inferior R margin of heart and apex to supply the RV and apex of heart
  • o Posterior interventricular artery (posterior descending artery) – runs within the posterior interventricular groove to
  • o the apex to supply the RV, LV and the posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum

AV nodal artery – passes from near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery to the AV node to supply it

  • L coronary artery: runs within the coronary sulcus

Anterior interventricular artery (L anterior descending artery) – passes along the anterior interventricular groove to

  • o the apex of the heart to supply the RV and LV and the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum

Will anastomose with the posterior interventricular artery branching off of the R coronary artery

  • §

Circumflex artery – continues in the coronary sulcus to the posterior surface of the heart to supply the LA and LV; gives

  • o rise to the L marginal artery

Will anastomose with the R coronary artery

blocks.html:
• Great cardiac vein – runs with the LAD and circumflex artery to drain into the coronary sinus
  • Middle cardiac vein – runs with the posterior interventricular artery to drain into the coronary sinus
  • Small cardiac vein – runs with the R coronary artery to drain into the coronary sinus
  • Coronary sinus (main vein) – runs left to right posteriorly in the coronary groove, receiving blood from the great, middle, and

small cardiac veins before draining into the RA

Coronary nerve supply
  • When electrical impulses are propagated throughout cardiac muscle tissue, the myocytes contract
  • Sinoatrial (SA) node(“pacemaker”): located in the R atrial wall at the junction of the SVC and RA
  • Atrioventricular (AV) node: located in the inferior portion of the interatrial septum; conducts impulses in one direction only
  • AV bundle (bundle of His): the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles; branches into R/L bundle branches
  • Purkinje fibres: large conduction myofibrils that become continuous with the muscle mass
  • Septomarginal trabecular(moderator band): runs from the inferior portion of the interventricular septum to the base of the

anterior papillary muscle in the RV and carries conduction fibres throughout the RV

  • Pathway of impulse conduction: SA node àAP produced and travels via three internodal tracts àAV node àBundle of His à
  • R/L bundle branches travel through the interventricular septum à apex of the heart àPurkinje fibres à ventricle contraction

blocks.html:
Extrinsic innervation to the heart
  • Sympathetics: cardiopulmonary splanchnics (T1-T4/5) send fibres from the sympathetic chain to the cardiac plexus

Cardiac plexus: a diffuse network of delicate nerve fibres extending from the trachea to the aortic arch

  • o Increases HR and force of contraction, and causes dilation of the coronary blood vessels
  • o General visceral afferents carry pain sensations from the heart (due to ischemia and accumulation of metabolic by-
  • o products) retrograde along the sympathetic nerves to the dorsal roots of T1-T4/5

Referred pain: the brain may misinterpret this as coming from the T1-T4/5 dermatomes

  • §

Phrenic nerves provide sensory innervation to the pericardial sac – pericarditis pain can be referred to C3-C5

  • §
  • Parasympathetics: primarily supplied by the vagus nerve

Decreases HR and force of contraction, and causes constriction of the coronary blood vessels

  • o Transmits cardiac reflexes responding to changes in tension/pressure (baroreceptors) or O2 levels (chemoreceptors)

blocks.html: Determinants of Cardiac Output

blocks.alt: Figure from the Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump notes

blocks.html:
Cardiac output (CO): amount of blood pumped in one minute; increases with oxygen demand (exercise, fever); normal =5 L/min

  • CO = HR × SV

Cardiac index: a haemodynamic parameter that relates heart performance to the size of the individual

  • Cardiac index = CO/body surface area, L/min/m2

Heart rate (HR): number of contractions in 1 min; normal resting HR = 70-80 bpm

  • Pacemaker of sinoatrial node sets HR; normal resting SA node = 110
  • Input from the parasympathetic nervous system decreases HR (vagus nerve) – athlete resting HR = 50-60 bpm
  • Input from the sympathetic nervous system increases HR
  • Heart transplants are denervated

No PSNS innervation – higher HR due to the intrinsic rate of the SA node

  • o No SNS innervation – catecholamines in the blood can cause tachycardia
  • Force-frequency relationship (Bowditch/treppe phenomenon): an increase in HR increases the force of contraction, but only up

to a maximum rate; not as effective for failing ventricles

  • Increases in HR decrease diastolic time, which results in decreased CO and decreased cardiac perfusion

blocks.alt: Figure from the Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump notes
Figure from the Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump notes

blocks.html:
Stroke volume (SV): amount of blood pumped in one contraction; normal = 60-70 mL

Preload (EDV): the amount of blood that fills the ventricles during diastole and stretches them to their greatest dimensions

  • Starling’s Law: the more a muscle fibre is stretched/lengthened, the greater its contractile energy

There is an optimal sarcomere length, and beyond the optimal length there is no increase in tension produced

  • o An increase in preload/EDV increases SV
  • Frank-Starling curves: show how changes in ventricular preload lead to changes in SV

blocks.alt: Figure from the Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump notes

blocks.html:
Changes in HR

  • Bradycardia = HR too low

-Low CO if SV does not increase

  • Tachycardia = HR too high

-Increased myocardial oxygen consumption,

decreased myocardial perfusion (occurs mainly

during diastole for the LV), decreased time for

diastolic filling; demand ischemia

  • Increasing age is associated with a decrease in

maximal HR (220 – age) and maximal oxygen

consumption, and stiffer aorta and ventricles

blocks.html: Determinants of Preload

rows:
A more compliant ventricle can hold more blood at a given pressure than a
noncompliant ventricle

Increased afterload increases preload; causes less blood to be pumped out
with contraction, which leaves more residual blood to add on to EDV
If more blood is pumped out in systole, less is around to add to the EDV
Atrial “kick” forces some additional blood into the ventricle from the atria
Excessive pressure in the thorax can reduce venous return to the RV

blocks.html:
Case Example

A previously healthy hockey player suffers an acute injury with blood loss and feels faint – what will the patient’s vital signs be like?

  • Heart rate: increased to help maintain CO
  • Blood pressure: initially maintained due to sympathetic nervous system, but then decreased due to blood loss
  • Oxygen saturation: normal, as the lungs are functioning
  • Respiratory rate: increased due to fear
  • Temperature: decreased, may start to become hypothermic, especially if given blood products
  • Urine output: decreased in order to preserve water and maintain circulating volume
How will the patient be compensating for the blood loss?
  • Reduced urine output and vasoconstriction to maintain SV
  • Decreased capillary refill will be seen as blood is being sent to the vital organs rather than the extremities
  • Stop the bleed (pressure); elevate the patient’s legs and give fluids or transfusions to help increase SV; surgical intervention

Afterload: the wall tension or stress the ventricle must develop to open the aortic valve and eject blood into the aorta

  • Law of Laplace: tension = (pressure × radius)/(wall thickness × 2)
  • Clinically simplified to pulmonary arterial pressure (right) or MAP (left)
  • RV = lower afterload – has to generate less pressure to eject blood
  • Can decrease afterload clinically by decreasing pressure – vasodilator, intra-

aortic balloon pump for LV failure; be cautious of hypotension

  • A normal heart tolerates changes to afterload well, but a failing heart is very

sensitive to afterload

  • Increased RV afterload: pulmonary embolism with R heart failure

Acute response: ventricular dilation, increase EDV + ESV, decrease SV

  • Increased LV afterload: hypertension – increasing aortic pressure

Chronic response: concentric hypertrophy, increase in wall thickness

  • o Good à compensatory, decreases afterload
  • o Bad à stiffer ventricle, more prone to ischemia/difficult to perfuse
  • o Hypertrophy: increase in ventricular mass and cell volume
  • 1. Physiologic: athlete’s heart – normal, lower HR; changes are reversible
  • 2. Concentric: pressure overload – increased relative wall thickness
  • 3. Eccentric (dilated): volume overload – normal relative wall thickness

blocks.alt: Figure from the Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump notes

blocks.html:
Ventricular remodeling: changes in mass, volume, and shape of the

ventricles as a compensatory response to an increased load

  • Occurs in myocardial infarction, hypertension, and valvular heart disease
  • Molecular mechanisms: aldosterone, angiotensin II, cytokines (TNF, IL-6)
  • Includes interstitial fibrosis, collagen deposition, and apoptosis

Clinical Relevance

  • EDV cannot be easily measured or monitored
  • If there is not enough EDV, the heart will be

underfilled

  • If there is too much EDV, the heart will be too

stretched, which can result in decompensation

of the ventricle, and increased LV diastolic

pressure and congestion (pulmonary edema)

  • A failing ventricle is less responsive to EDV

Microcirculation
  • Macrocirculation: transports material carried in the blood between organs – long distances, movement within vessels
  • Microcirculation: distributes and exchanges material within organs – short distances, movement within capillaries

blocks.alt: Figure from the Microcirculation notes

blocks.html:
Bulk flow: the movement of fluid along a vessel due to a pressure gradient

  • Resistance to flow – geometry of the vessel, viscosity of the blood

Diffusion: the movement of material across a vessel wall due to a concentration gradient

  • Factors affecting diffusion to tissues: blood flow, concentration gradient, endothelial area, endothelial permeability
  • Fick principle: increased flow leads to more arterial oxygen available/min, which can increase exchange by diffusion (dO2/dt)

Uptake = flow × ([arterial O2] – [venous O2])

  • o Used to assess CO by measuring arterial and venous O2 levels
  • Multi-directional flow in adjacent capillaries enhances uniform exchange
  • The lung is an ideal exchange organ due to its large surface area, short diffusion distances, and fast flow

𝝅𝑷𝐫𝟒

𝟖𝜼𝒍

Poiseuille’s law: 𝑸=

𝟖𝜼𝒍 or𝐑=

𝝅𝐫𝟒

  • Blood flow in vessels is generally laminar
  • When blood enters a smaller vessel, a parabolic blood profile develops
  • Plasma skimming: the natural separation of RBCs from plasma at bifurcations in the vascular

tree, dividing the blood into relatively concentrated and relatively dilute streams; results in

low hematocrit entering the smaller capillaries

  • Factors increasing turbulence: low/high blood viscosity (disrupt laminar flow), vessel

obstructions (increased CO in pregnancy, atherosclerotic plaques, stenotic heart valves)

Hematocrit: volume of blood occupied by packed RBCs; men = 45%, women = 40%

  • Alters blood viscosity 3-4× that of water; provides basis for laminar flow
  • Low hematocrit: not enough O2 carrying capacity per volume
  • High hematocrit: viscosity is too high to provide adequate blood flow
  • Optimal O2 delivery occurs when the hematocrit/viscosity ratio is maximized

• Case Example

A 30 year female fell from 3rd floor balcony and sustained displacement of C5/C6.

  • No other major injuries
  • Previously well, no medications

On exam:

  • BP = 70/30, HR = 45, RR = 26, temperature = 37.0, oxygen saturation = 96% on room air, urine output < 20 cc/hr
  • No movement or sensation below collar line
Why is she in shock and what type of shock is this?
  • Neurogenic shock, resulting in injury to the spinal cord associated with autonomic dysregulation – C5/C6 à T1-T4 is critical for sympathetic outflow
  • Loss of sympathetic tone with an unopposed parasympathetic response
  • Chronic blood pressure control = renal and hormonal mechanismsàslow response
  • Aldosterone helps regulate blood volume, BP, and levels of Na+, K+, and H+ in the blood
  • Increased K+ in extracellular fluid stimulates the adrenal cortex to increase aldosterone production

34.What is the function and organization of the circulatory system?

Function: transport materials required by cells; transport hormones and metabolites; transfer heat from the core of the body to the surface; remove

nitrogenous wastes and CO2 from the body

Organization: cardiopulmonary circulation (in series), systemic circulation (in parallel); arterial system (high pressure), venous system (low pressure)

Overall goal is to provide blood flow to organs in response to their needs

35.What are the properties and functions of the vessels that comprise the circulatory system?

Elastic arteries – closest to the heart; have the most elastin to withstand high pressure and recoil

Muscular arteries – have less elastin and more smooth muscle content

Arterioles – contain significant smooth muscle content

Capillary beds – link arterioles and venules

Venules, veins – move blood back to the heart

36.What is the role of capillaries? Lined by a single layer of cells and allow diffusion of materials from both the capillary to surrounding tissues and vice-

versa; are in direct contact with single-cell layered alveolar sacs in the lungs

42.What is the difference between laminar blood flow and turbulent blood flow?

Laminar flow: characterized by the slowest blood flow occurring closest to the vessel wall, with increasing velocities to the center of the vessel

Turbulent flow: disorganized blood flow that occurs at points of vessel obstruction; flow rate is decreased, perfusion pressure is increased

43.What increases turbulence? Low blood viscosity, high blood viscosity

44.How can the hematocrit affect blood viscosity and vessel resistance? Hematocrit contributes to the viscosity of blood, which is why blood flow is laminar;

  • resistance is directly proportional to viscosity à if blood viscosity increases to an abnormally high hematocrit, resistance in the vessel would also increase;

in anemia, reduced hematocrit results in reduced resistance

45.What is the difference between acute and chronic blood pressure regulation? What are the pathways and components of each?

  • Acute BP regulation is neuronally controlled and is able to respond rapidly to changes in BP àbaroreceptors
  • Chronic BP regulation involves hormonal regulation through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system à primary role of the kidneys

46.What role to AVP and ANP play in blood pressure regulation?

AVP: dehydration is detected due to increased extracellular osmolality; AVP released from the posterior pituitary, which increases water permeability in

  • the collecting ducts of the kidney and increases water reabsorption àincreases blood volume and increases blood pressure

ANP: peptide hormone released by atrial muscle cells in response to increased stretch resulting from increased blood volume, which increases the GFR

  • in the kidney and decreases sodium reabsorption in the collecting ducts àdecreases blood volume and decreases blood pressure

47.How is blood flow controlled by:

Metabolites? Metabolic hypothesis – vasodilator metabolites regulate vascular tone

Autoregulation? Constant blood flow over a wide range of blood pressures

Active regulation? Occurs in response to changes in blood flow reflecting metabolic demand

Reactive regulation? Occurs “after the fact”

48.What is reactive hyperemia? Occurs when blood flow in a vessel stops; when blood flow is resumed, blood flow is increased above the pre-blockage level

49.How do vascular smooth muscle cells regulate vasoconstriction and vasodilation?

Vasoconstriction: increased intracellular calcium initiates a second messenger signalling pathway that results in decreased GMP in the cells

Vasodilation: decreased intracellular calcium leads to increased cGMP

  • What role does nitric oxide play? NO maintains high concentrations of cGMP in smooth muscle cells by increasing guanylyl cyclase activity (GTP à cGMP)

Digoxin
  • Drug with a narrow therapeutic window – toxic threshold
  • Long t1/2 (36 hours) in patients with normal kidney function; longer with kidney dysfunction since it is renally excreted
  • Many drug interactions, which may result in an increase in digoxin levels
  • No effect on overall mortality, but associated with fewer admissions for pulmonary edema (decreased morbidity)

Case Example
Jurassic Park (1993) – The Sick Triceratops
  • Confusion and disorientation
  • Dilated pupils
  • Dry mouth
  • Not sweating
  • Enlarged abdomen – ileus, distended bladder

This is pharmacologic

  • a) Sympathomimetic: increased HR/BP, dilated pupils, CNS changes, sweating
  • b) Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: muscarinic effects (sweating, nausea/vomiting, secretions); nicotinic effects (variable HR/BP, muscle weakness/paralysis)
  • c) Muscarinic agonist: SLUDGE, constricted pupils, decreased HR
  • d) Nicotine poisoning: dry mouth, dilated pupils, paralysis
  • e) Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic): dry mouth, dilated pupils, not sweating/dry skin, ileus/bladder distension, confusion/disorientation, increased HR/BP

Meet the Patient

Howard is a 72 year old man who presents to the Emergency Department with exertional breathlessness. This has been apparent and progressively worsened

over the preceding 2 months. He has been aware of occasional palpitations but has had no chest pain. He feels more breathless when lying flat, but this is eased

when sitting up. He has a cough that is not associated with sputum production and has had no fevers, weight loss or any other notable symptoms or concerns.

History

Medical history: Past medical history includes hypertension for approximately 5 years but is otherwise unremarkable. He does not have diabetes or dyslipidemia.

He stopped smoking approximately 40 years ago.

Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg/day
Allergies: Penicillin (rash)

Social history: Lives with wife, fully independent. Retired accountant. Occasional glass of wine. Stopped smoking 40 years ago (prior 5-10/day for 10 years).

Examination

Alert and orientated. Afebrile, Generally well, seems short of breath when talking.

Vitals: HR = 150 bpm; BP = 125/75 mm Hg; respiratory rate = 20/min; oxygen saturations = 92% (on room air)

Cardiac exam: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, elevated jugular venous pressure, mild swelling of the ankles.

Respiratory exam: Fine crackles at both bases. Lung fields resonant to percussion except for the bases which are dull to percussion.

There are multiple possible investigations that could be done. What would be the priority with regard to immediate management?

  • a) ECG: Yes – to accurately record the rate, determine the rhythm and may give clues to cardiac structural abnormalities
  • b) CXR: Yes – to confirm or refute the suggestion from Hx/PEx findings of volume overload and exclude other pathologies causing breathlessness (pneumonia)
  • c) CT Pulmonary Angiogram: No – unless clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism is elevated for some other reason not given in the Hx/PEx
  • d) Bloodwork: Yes – may be helpful to exclude precipitating causes
  • e) Coronary angiogram: No – he has no chest pain or other reason to suggest that an immediate coronary angiogram is going to be helpful
ECG

blocks.alt: Figure from the Case of the Week notes

blocks.html:
You choose to do an ECG. What does it show? Tick all that apply.

  • Tachycardia: Yes
  • Bradycardia: No – the ECG shows a tachycardia
  • Atrial fibrillation: No – although the rhythm is irregularly irregular, there are flutter waves consistent with atrial flutter
  • Atrial flutter: Yes – there are “flutter waves”
  • Atrial tachycardia: No – there are visible flutter waves
  • Ventricular tachycardia: No – the complexes are narrow
  • Acute myocardial infarction: No – there are no clues to acute myocardial infarction on this ECG
Chest X-Ray Report
Clinical Information
  • Short of breath
Findings
  • There are no previous for comparison
  • The heart is mildly prominent
  • There are small pleural effusions bilaterally, and there are increased interstitial markings in both lower lungs, suggesting the results of cardiac

decompensation

Summary
  • Interstitial pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions
Bloodwork

Bloodwork is ordered and is as follows:

  • CBC: HB = 147g/L, Lkc = 10 x 109/L, Plt = 243 x109/L
  • Na = 136 mmol/L , K = 3.7 mmol/L, Urea = 9.3 mmol/L, creatinine = 76 umol/L
  • TSH = 3.40 mIU/L

Normal ranges:

  • HB (135-170 g/L)
  • LKC (4.0-10.0 × 10*9/L)
  • Plt (150-400 × 10*9/L)
  • Na (135-145 mmol/L)
  • K+ (3.5- 5.0 mmol/L)
  • Urea (< 11.9 mmol/L)
  • Creat (62-120 mmol/L)
  • TSH (0.27-4.2 mIU/L)

His baseline bloodwork is within normal limits. Why is it essential to perform these investigations prior to treatment?

  • a) Electrolyte disturbances can cause abnormalities of cardiac rhythms: True
  • b) Thyroid function abnormalities can cause abnormalities of cardiac rhythm: True – in particular thyrotoxicosis can cause atrial arrhythmias
  • c) Anemia can cause tachycardia: True
  • d) Anemia may cause problems with the management: True
  • e) Elevated white blood cell (leukocyte) count may raise concern for another illness such as infection: True – often atrial fibrillation may present at the same

time as another illness in particular infections such as pneumonia

You conclude that he has atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response with heart failure. What are the priorities of management?

  • a) Correction of the rhythm: No – this doesn’t have to occur immediately
  • b) Correction of the rate: True – reduction of ventricular rate is likely to be helpful
  • c) Treatment of the heart failure: True – initial treatment will include diuretics to relieve the congestion
  • d) Anticoagulation: True – ideally, he will be treated with anticoagulation to reduce the risk of thromboembolism with his atrial fibrillation; it is important to

know that the patient is not anemic prior to commencement of anticoagulation

He is given some oxygen and diuretics and feels a little better. What are the options for heart rate control?

  • a) Beta blocker (e.g. metoprolol): Yes, with caution – beta blockers are excellent for ventricular rate control, but are also negative inotropes and so must be

given with caution (low doses initially) in heart failure

  • b) Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (e.g. Diltiazem): No – can be used to rate control, but negative inotropic effects render them not first choice
  • c) Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine): No – has vasodilatory role, but no rate limiting activity
  • d) Digoxin: Yes – reasonable choice initially when the patient is acutely unwell as not negatively inotropic, but would ideally be substituted with a beta blocker

when the patient has improved

Case Wrap-Up

The patient is treated in the Emergency Department with diuretics and excess fluid is relieved. His ventricular rate is improved with beta blockers. He is treated

with anticoagulation to reduce the risk of thromboembolism.

With diuresis and rate control, the patient improved. He was discharged home on beta blocker, oral furosemide, oral anticoagulation, and an ACE inhibitor. He

was asked to follow-up with his family physician in 2 weeks to recheck his electrolytes and renal function on these new medications. An outpatient follow-up

appointment was arranged with cardiology in 2 months with plans for an echocardiogram for assessment of cardiac function.

Module Questions
  • 1. When you hear an S1, which valves are closing? Mitral, tricuspid
  • 2. You are auscultating the precordium of a patient with uncontrolled hypertension for many years. You hear a normal S1 and S2 and an additional late
  • diastolic sound. What is the extra sound? S4à often present in patients with “stiff” or pressure loaded left ventricles
  • 3. You hear a murmur loudest at the apex. It is a diastolic murmur. It sounds like a rumble. The apex beat is hard to palpate. What is the likely cause of the
  • murmur? Mitral stenosisà low-pitched rumble heard in diastole; apex beat can often be challenging to palpate because there is less blood entering the LV
  • 4. You hear a murmur in systole loudest at the base. Which of the following (tricuspid regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation)

could be the cause of the murmur? Aortic stenosis

  • 5. You hear a murmur a systolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla and there is an S3. The apex beat is displaced laterally. What is the likely cause

of the murmur? Mitral regurgitation

Investigations in Cardiovascular Disease
Ischemia: insufficient blood supply to a specific organ

The ischemic cascade

  • First detectable abnormality is a perfusion abnormality at the cellular level
  • Abnormalities of ventricular function
  • Abnormalities detected on an ECG – ischemic ST depression
  • Angina: chest pain related to myocardial ischemia, caused by coronary arterial narrowing/reduced blood flow to the heart

Hx and PEx are the most important investigations for ischemic heart disease

  • Testing is NOT recommended in asymptomatic, low-risk patients à use Framingham risk score
  • Severe CAD requiring intervention in asymptomatic patients are rare
  • False positive tests result in: inappropriate anxiety, adverse consequences related to work and insurance, complications from

further diagnostic testing

rows:
Predictors of CAD:
• Age, male gender, chest pain symptoms – most powerful
• Diabetes, smoking (½ ppd), hypercholesterolemia, ECG changes (Q waves, STT changes)
Framingham risk score: estimated 10-year CVD risk, based on age, sex, smoking status, total cholesterol, HDL, and systolic BP
• Low risk (< 10%): lifestyle interventions, retest in 5 years with risk estimation
• Intermediate risk (10-19%): lifestyle interventions, moderate-potency statin
• High risk (≥ 20%): lifestyle interventions, high-potency statin, consider ASA

Angina pectoris: substernal squeezing chest pain (5-30 minutes); occurs with stress, emotion, or physical activity; relieved with
rest or nitroglycerin
Levine sign: chest hand-clutching; the universal sign of distress in angina pectoris and myocardial infarction; pain > 20 minutes

Used to assess electrical activity; important tool in diagnosis of myocardial ischemia or infarction
ECG may be normal or nonspecific
Classic angina: normal, ST segment depression and T wave abnormalities, Q waves
STEMI: ST elevation, T wave inversions, Q waves, LBBB
NSTEMI: ST segment depression and T wave inversions
Limitations:
• Potential underdiagnosis: normal ECG does not exclude myocardial ischemia/infarction; normal ECG throughout course of acute
MI uncommon; leads to undertreatment
• Potential overdiagnosis: ST elevations from other conditions – acute pericarditis, acute myocarditis, Brugada syndrome, early
repolarization (normal), Prinzmetal’s angina; exposes patient to unneeded risk from overtreatment

Complete blood count: hemoglobin
Renal function: creatinine, microalbumin (especially if using contrast)
Electrolytes: Na+, K+
Glucose: diabetes, HbA 1c
Hypercholesterolemia: LDL HDL, apolipoprotein B-100 (ApoB; main protein in LDL; not in ER)
High sensitivity reactive protein: hs-CRP (inflammation marker; atherosclerosis)
Cardiac biomarkers reflect acute damage to the myocardium; chemicals/enzymes are irreversibly released from injured muscle
cells over a period of hours-days
•Troponin (acute chest pain) – initial rise = 2-4 hours, peak = 12 hours, normal 5-10 days; larger MI = longer detection in blood;
most sensitive and specific for myocardial injury; can be elevated by contusion, myocarditis, stretch from PE, and arrhythmias
•Creatinine kinase (CK-MB) – peak = 10-24 hours; specific if no skeletal injury
•LDH – peak = 24-72 hours
•Myoglobin – peak = 2 hours; low specificity for MI

blocks.html:
Case Example

A 41-year-old man presents to you for a minor medical problem. He has not seen a GP in years.

  • Asymptomatic in terms of chest pain or shortness of breath
  • Non-smoker, no family history
  • BP = 128/76 mm Hg, normal cardiac exam
  • ECG normal

He asks you about doing some heart tests to look for “blockages in his heart”. What test would you order to determine if he has CAD?

  • None à low pretest probability – Hx/PEx unremarkable, labwork normal (lipid profile, glucose, creatinine), low Framingham risk score, ECG normal;

reassurance on lifestyle changes

The patient returns 4 years later with atypical chest pain, hypertension (BP = 148/86 mm Hg), and hypercholesterolemia. What test would you now consider

given his increased cardiovascular risk?

  • Stress test

Suppose the patient has a bad knee and is unable to walk on a treadmill. What test would you now consider?

  • Persantine – MIBI

His chest pain is now affecting his quality of life. He gets both it and shortness of breath with walking 1 flight of stairs. His non-invasive study was high-risk (MIBI

showed large area reversible ischemia). What test would you now consider?

  • Coronary angiogram

Suppose the patient developed sudden onset substernal chest pressure lasting 2 hours before calling EMS and being taken to the ER, where you are asked to

assess him. His ECG shows an anterior STEMI. What blood tests would you initially order?

  • CBC; electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine; glucose; troponin

After sustaining his MI, what investigation will provide the optimal information regarding the strongest predictor for his long-term survival?

  • 2D echocardiogram – MUGA

Pharmacologic stress test agents
  • Vasodilators

Persantine (dipyridamole): inhibits cellular uptake of adenosine; ↑ adenosine levels and binding to adenosine receptors

  • o Contraindications: sick sinus syndrome (AV block), bronchospastic airway disease (asthma)

Contraindications: sustained ventricular arrhythmias, recent MI, severe hypertension (SBP > 128 mm Hg)

• Suspected purulent pericardial effusion
Diagnostic:
• Large effusions where Dx of malignancy or
infection suspected

Treat the heart failure:
• Diuretics, low salt diet
Treat underlying inflammation:
• Especially if pericardial late gadolinium
enhancement on MRI
• NSAIDs/colchicine/steroids/anakinra (IL1

Surgical pericardiectomy

blocks.html:
Case Example

A 32-year-old man is experiencing sharp chest pain that is worse with inspiration and when he lays down. He is only comfortable sitting up and leaning forward.

He isn’t having any shortness of breath, palpitations, light-headedness, or fainting. He recently had two days of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. He doesn’t have

any prior medical issues. He doesn’t take any medications. No allergies. No smoking/marijuana/alcohol/IV drugs. No family history.

On exam:

  • BP = 124/56 mm Hg (similar in both arms), HR = 95 bpm, O2 saturation = 99%, RR = 20/min, afebrile
  • When you listen to his precordium, you hear a scratchy sound in systolic and diastole
  • His JVP is normal, no pedal edema, chest clear, no skin rashes, no inflamed joints

Tests to order:

  • Labwork: WBC = 17 (elevated), troponin normal, ESR = 65 (elevated), CRP = 15 (elevated)
  • ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression, PR elevation (AVR)

blocks.alt: Figure from the Pericardial Disease notes

blocks.html:
• CXR: normal
  • Echocardiogram: trace pericardial effusion

Diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis:

Need 2 of:

  • Pleuritic chest pain
  • Pericardial rub
  • New widespread ST elevation or PR interval depression
  • Pericardial effusion

Diagnosis: acute pericarditis in the setting of viral illness

Case Example

A 55-year-old woman is experiencing progressive shortness of breath – previously with exertion and now at rest. She is not experiencing swelling of her ankles,

chest pain or palpitations. She feels light-headed when she is walking. She has not fainted. She has had a “nagging” cough for the last 6 months, sometimes

coughing up blood. She attributes this cough to a “smoker’s cough”. She has lost weight, about 15 lbs, unintentionally recently. She does not have fevers or night

sweats. No recent illnesses. She doesn’t take any medications. No allergies.

On exam:

  • Looks uncomfortable
  • BP = 85/73 mm Hg, HR = 120 bpm, O2 saturation = 95%, RR = 38/min, afebrile
  • Her JVP is elevated
  • You have a hard time hearing her heart sounds – they sound muffled; her chest is clear

Tests to order:

  • ECG: sinus tachycardia, electrical alternans
  • CXR: ↑ cardiac silhouette
  • Echocardiogram: large pericardial effusion, swinging heart, echo signs of tamponade

Management:

  • Urgent bedside pericardiocentesis
  • Fluid – bloody, low glucose, fluid to serum LDH = 0.8 (high), protein (high, malignancy)
  • Cytology – lung adenocarcinoma
  • CT chest – mass consistent with lung adenocarcinoma
Module Questions

48.List 4 causes of pericarditis. Viral/bacterial infections, lupus, metastatic tumours, renal failure, post-pericardiotomy syndrome, chemotherapy agents

49.Which of the following (pericardial rub, ST elevation in the inferior leads only, chest heaviness, elevated troponin) is part of the diagnostic criteria for acute

  • pericarditis? Pericardial rubà also pleuritic chest pain, new widespread ST elevation or PR depression on ECG, and pericardial effusion

50.You are assessing a patient with suspected cardiac tamponade. List the physical exam findings present in Beck’s triad. Low BP, high JVP, muffled heart

sounds

51.List 4 common causes of constrictive pericarditis. Pericarditis, idiopathic, post-cardiotomy, chest irradiation (mantle radiation for lymphoma),

rheumatologic (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus), end-stage renal disease, malignancy, TB (most common in developing countries)

Additional supportive criteria:

  • Elevated markers of inflammation
  • Pericardial inflammation on CT or MRI

Endocarditis
  • Endocarditis: infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, one or more heart valves, or an indwelling cardiac device, with

local collection of fibrinous material and superimposed infection

rows:
Incidence between 1970-2000: 5-7 cases per 100 000 person-years
Incidence since 2000: 15 cases per 100 000 person-years
Male, mean age = 67 year
Younger patients – developing countries, underprivileged socioeconomic demographic

Cardiac related:
• Congenital heart disease: bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, ventricular septal defect
• Acquired valvular heart disease: rheumatic heart disease, previous endocarditis, prosthetic cardiac valves
Patient related: immunocompromised, IVDU, indwelling vascular catheters or devices, septicemia
Potentially infective procedures: dental procedures, body piercing, skin wounds, systemic sepsis, genitourinary instrumentation, endoscopies

Microorganisms (native valve):
• Streptococcus – S. pneumoniae, S. bovis
• Staphylococcus aureus
• Enterococcus
• HACEK organisms (7-21 day incubation time) – Haemophilus parainfluenza, Haemophilus aphrophilus, Haemophilus paraphrophilus;
Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans; Cardiobacterium hominis; Eikenella corrodens; Kingella kingae
• Culture negative – Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), Bartonella quintana, Brucella, Chlamydia, Legionella, Tropheryma whipplei
Microorganisms (prosthetic valve):
• Early (< 60 days): CNST > S. aureus > G-ve bacilli > Enterococcus = fungi =
diphtheroids > HACEK > polymicrobial > Streptococcus spp
• Intermediate: CNST > S. aureus = Enterococcus = fungi > Streptococcus spp >
HACEK = polymicrobial > G-ve bacilli = diphtheroids
• Late (> 60 days): Streptococcus spp > S. aureus > CNST > Enterococcus >
G-ve bacilli = HACEK = polymicrobial > diphtheroids > fungi
Microorganisms (IVDU): S. aureus, G-ve rods, usually tricuspid valve (R side)
Normal valvular endothelium is smooth and resistant to bacterial colonization
Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (damage to vascular surface):
• Systemic disease states (rheumatic carditis)
• Mechanical injury by catheters or electrodes
• Injury arising from repeated injections of solid particles in IVDU
Transient bacteremia
Microorganism–NBTE interaction
Platelet aggregation and evolution of the vegetation
Biofilm formation – makes it more resistant to antibiotic therapy

Generalà level of consciousness, mental status, vitals
HEENTà fundoscopy for Roth’s spots, conjunctival hemorrhage, neck
stiffness, oral mucosal petechia
CNS: stroke, focal neurological symptoms – may indicate that
vegetations have spread systemically à full neuro exam
Cardiac: CHF (dyspnea, ankle edema, PND) à JVP, S3, regurgitant
murmur, volume status
Respiratory: septic emboli to lungs (cough, sputum production) à
signs of pneumonia
MSK: septic emboli to joints (joint pain) à joint exam
GU: hematuria
GI: bloody diarrhea from septic emboli, abdominal pain à
hepatosplenomegaly, masses
Peripheral septic emboli (skin rash) à clubbing splinter hemorrhages,
Osler nodes (painful), Janeway lesions

Acute: fulminant septic illness with emboli, valve destruction, and
cardiac decompensation
Subacute: non-specific constitutional symptoms, anorexia/ weight
loss, fevers/chills/night sweats, fatigue/general malaise, flu-like
illness, cardiac decompensation (shortness of breath, edema)

Peripheral stigmata: septic emboli, finger clubbing, subungual
hematoma, splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots, Janeway lesions
Cardiac decomposition: tachycardia, new murmur, peripheral edema,
weight gain (fluid retention), pulmonary edema
Sepsis: fever, organ-specific infective syndromes secondary to emboli

With bacteremia: intravascular catheter infection, cardiac device infection, prosthetic joint infection, hematogenous osteomyelitis, septic
thrombophlebitis, infected arterial aneurysm
Without bacteremia: systemic lupus erythematosus, Hodgkin’s disease

rows:
Bloodwork: CBC, coagulation, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, cancer antigen profile, liver enzymes, lactate, albumin cardiac enzymes, ESR,
complement, rheumatoid factor
Pan-culture: 3 blood cultures for extended growth (2 bottles, 3 sites, 3 times in the first hour if very sick), urine culture, sputum culture
ECG and CXR – may show signs of conduction disease that may go along with abscess formation or septic emboli
Echocardiogram (as soon as possible after Dx of IE is suspected):
• Evaluate valvular dysfunction, assess hemodynamic severity of the valve lesions, assess underlying ventricular function, detect associated
abnormalities (shunts), follow-up evaluation of patients with persistent or recurrent bacteremia, other clinical deterioration
• False-negative results may be obtained if vegetations are small or have embolized
• Warranted even for patients with an associated condition that requires a protracted course of antimicrobial therapy – vertebral osteomyelitis
TTE: first diagnostic test; sensitivity = 70%, specificity = 99+%
TEE: sensitivity > 90% for detection of valvular vegetation
• Superior for detection of cardiac complications (abscess, leaflet perforation, aortic pseudoaneurysm, intracardiac fistula)
• Negative or technically inadequate TTE with high clinical suspicion
• Concern for the presence of intracardiac complications
• Significant valvular regurgitation to determine the need for surgery
• Cardiac device and persistent fever – even without new murmur or bacteremia

Duke’s criteria
• Definite IE: 2 major criteria, 1 major criterion + 3 minor criteria, 5 minor criteria
• Possible IE: 1 major criterion + 1 minor criterion, 3 minor criteria
• IE rejected: firm alternative Dx present, signs/symptoms resolve with 4 days of antibiotic therapy, absence of pathological evidence for IE at
the time of surgery (with 4 days of antibiotic therapy), criteria for possible IE are not met

Major criteria
• Positive blood culture for IE with a typical organism from 2 separate
blood cultures
• Persistently positive- blood cultures for any organism (at least 2
positive cultures of samples drawn > 12 h apart)
• Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or anti-phase IgG
antibody titer of > 1:800
• Echocardiogram positive for IE including vegetation, abscess, new
partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve, or new valve regurgitation

Minor criteria
• Predisposing heart condition or IVDU
• Fever ≤ 38°C
• Vascular phenomena: arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts,
mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival
hemorrhages, Janeway lesions
• Microbiological evidence that does not meet major criteria
• Positive blood culture not meeting major criteria
• Immunological phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid
factor, glomerulonephritis

Antibiotics – 6-12 weeks of IV antibiotics
• Native valve endocarditis: IV vancomycin, IV cefepime
• Prosthetic valve endocarditis: IV vancomycin, IV cefepime
• Culture-negative endocarditis: IV vancomycin, IV ceftriaxone, IV gentamicin or doxycycline
Surgery
• Heart failure: valve dysfunction or intracardiac fistula causing pulmonary edema or
cardiogenic shock
• Persistent infection: enlarging vegetation or persistent bacteremia despite appropriate
antibiotic therapy
• Complication of infection: local uncontrolled infection resulting in abscess, heart block, or
penetrating lesion
• Prevention of embolism: mobile vegetation > 10 mm, especially when involving the
anterior mitral leaflet and in the setting of a previous embolic episode

Amoxicillin or clindamycin with a penicillin allergy
•Dental procedures: dental extractions; subgingival scaling; manipulation of the gingival tissue, periapical region of teeth, or oral mucosa
• High-risk patients: prosthetic heart valve/valve repair, prior endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease or residual shunt
• Moderate-risk procedures: unoperated heart valve disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

blocks.html:
Case Example

A 55-year-old man presented to hospital with fatigue, weight loss, and back pain. Blood cultures showed Viridans group streptococcus. Imaging showed

osteomyelitis of L2-L3. Started on ceftriaxone 2 g daily. Began showing clinical signs of biventricular failure.

Findings:

  • Mildly dilated LV with normal systolic function; mildly dilated RV with normal systolic function
  • Thickened mitral valve
  • Large (24 mm × 4 mm) mobile echodensities consistent with vegetations
  • Moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation
  • Thickened aortic cusps with large (15 mm × 5 mm) mobile echodensity in association with the L coronary cusp
  • Large central orifice secondary to aortic valve cusp destruction
  • Severe aortic regurgitation

Course in hospital:

  • Stroke – CT showed multifocal hemorrhages of the R parietotemporal lobe secondary to septic emboli with hemorrhagic transformation;

MRI showed R parietal hemorrhages with possible small mycotic aneurysm

  • Surgery – aortic and mitral valve replacement; abscess formation of the mitral valve leaflet
  • Prolonged corrected QT interval (QTc) and an episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; ICD implanted

Meet the Patient

A 48 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with worsening dyspnea. He describes symptoms of increasing exertional dyspnea, peripheral edema,

and orthopnea progressive over 2 months. He saw his family physician 2 weeks ago and was prescribed antibiotics for a presumed lower respiratory tract

infection. He describes limiting symptoms of dyspnea with minimal exertion.

History
  • Appendectomy age 18
  • Diabetes Mellitus: diagnosed 1 year ago; takes Metformin 500 mg BID
  • Seasonal allergies: takes over the counter cetirizine
  • Lives with his wife in a rural community about an hour away from the hospital
  • Smokes 10-15 CPD for last 30 years
Examination
  • He appears diaphoretic and tachypneic at rest
  • Pulse = 110 bpm; BP = 102/64 mm Hg; RR = 24/min
  • SpO2 = 89% on room air, 94% on 2 L supplemental O2 by nasal prongs
  • Temperature = 36.6C
  • Normal S1, diminished S2, no S3/S4 heard. III/IV late peaking systolic murmur at the left sternal border, with a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur

loudest in the 3rd/4th intercostal space. Carotid pulse is diminished with slow upstroke. Brachio-radial delay is noted in the upper extremities. JVP is 6 cm

above the sternal angle. 1+ peripheral edema in the lower extremities bilaterally.

  • Chest: equal expansion bilaterally, widespread crackles with mild wheeze noted
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly or masses
  • Neuro: alert, oriented; no focal neurologic deficits
He was then asked to undergo further testing
Test Results
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia 110 bpm, LVH criteria; no Q waves or significant ST changes
  • CXR: cardiomegaly, prominent pulmonary vasculature in the upper lobes (vascular redistribution), with Kerley B lines
  • Labs: CBC = normal, creatinine and electrolytes = normal; troponin = 80 (14)
  • ABG: pH = 7.38, PO2 = 65 mm Hg, PCO2 = 40 mm Hg, HCO3 = 23 mEq/L

This patient’s volume status is:

  • a) Normal/euvolemic
  • b) Overloaded/hypervolemic: Yes – this is suggested by the history and confirmed by the clinical examination findings of elevated venous pressure,

crepitations heard in the lung fields and peripheral edema

  • c) Contracted/hypovolemic
What is the most likely valve pathology in this patient?
  • a) Rheumatic mitral valve disease – mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation
  • b) Bicuspid aortic valve disease – aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation: the findings of late peaking systolic murmur, diminished second heart sounds,

diminished carotid upstroke and brachio-radial delay are findings of significant aortic stenosis; early diastolic decrescendo murmur loudest in the 3rd/4th

intercostal space is consistent with aortic regurgitation

  • c) Carcinoid heart disease – pulmonic stenosis and tricuspid regurgitation
  • d) Endocarditis of the mitral and aortic valves – aortic and mitral regurgitation
  • e) Endocarditis of the tricuspid and pulmonic valves – tricuspid and pulmonic regurgitation

What is the preferred diagnostic test for evaluation of this patient’s findings?

  • a) Coronary angiogram – may subsequently be helpful if it were determined that this were a myocardial problem and would help distinguish ischemic vs non-

ischemic causes

  • b) Transthoracic echocardiogram – he is presenting with heart failure and echocardiography will enable you to determine if this is related to a ventricular or

valvular problem; transthoracic echocardiogram is preferred over transesophageal as it is non-invasive

  • c) Transesophageal echocardiogram
  • d) Treadmill stress ECG – currently he appears breathless at rest and would be unable to perform the test; would likely be non-diagnostic
  • e) Nuclear myocardial perfusion scan – would not be able to exclude valvular disease
  • f) Cardiac MRI – could determine ventricular from valvular disease, but currently he is unable to lie flat and this would be necessary to undergo the test

Initial management should include (pick TWO of the following):

  • Supplemental oxygen by face mask – he is hypoxic
  • Non-invasive ventilation (bi-pap)
  • Intubation and ventilation
  • Intravenous diuretic – he is volume overloaded
  • Beta-blockade – he is tachycardic (a physiological response to heart failure) and attempts to rate control him with beta-blocker presently could lead to

further decompensation

  • Intravenous nitroglycerin – can be helpful in heart failure, but would be contraindicated in patients with severe aortic stenosis

He improves with your initial management and his echo report comes back and concludes: low-normal LV systolic function (LVEF 50-55%) with a bicuspid aortic

valve with severe stenosis and moderate regurgitation

What should be your next step in managing this patient?
  • a) Discharge from the ED with oral furosemide and refer to GP for follow up
  • b) Discharge from the ED with oral furosemide and refer to Cardiology for follow up
  • c) Admit to hospital for further investigation – he should not be discharged; the patient is clinically in heart failure and will require diuresis and workup of his

valvular heart disease

He is admitted, further diuresed and then undergoes cardiac catheterization. He is found to have an 80% stenosis in the proximal left anterior descending artery

and a 90% stenosis in the mid right coronary artery.

Which of the following should this patient be referred for?

  • a) Percutaneous coronary intervention to the LAD and RCA – will not fix the presenting dominant problem of valvular disease alone
  • b) Refer him for percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty – only offers temporary improvement in aortic stenosis and this man also has moderate aortic

regurgitation that may be worsened by this procedure

  • c) Refer him for PCI to LAD and RCA and percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty
  • d) Refer him for transcutaneous aortic valve implantation (TAVI) – a good procedure but currently is not appropriate for him as he is young and valve life

expectancy is short

  • e) Refer him for PCI and TAVI
  • f) Refer him for cardiac surgery for aortic valve replacement and coronary artery bypass
Surgical Consult

The patient sees a surgeon regarding aortic valve replacement and is told that there are two types – mechanical and bioprosthetic. He wonders which one would

be better.

What are differences between mechanical and bioprosthetic valves? List several possible complications related to both mechanical and bioprosthetic valves.

Mechanical valves are more “durable” and long lasting in nature; however, they do require chronic anticoagulation with warfarin. Younger patients should be

primarily considered for mechanical valves unless there are contraindications to anticoagulation.

Following Surgery

The patient gets a mechanical aortic valve and CABG performed. He feels much better. Two months later he develops ongoing fevers and chills.

What is a likely diagnosis?

Prosthetic valve endocarditis can be early or late. The patient needs blood cultures and an echocardiogram, possibly a transesophageal echo.

Atherosclerosis

Atherosclerosis: a systemic disease of large and medium-sized arteries, in which plaque (fatty substances, cholesterol, cellular waste

products, calcium, fibrin) builds up slowly, over decades in the inner lining of the arteries, causing them to thicken or harden

blocks.alt: Figure from the Atherosclerosis notes

blocks.html:
• Tunica intima (inner layer): single layer of epithelia cells; where atherosclerosis occurs
  • Tunica media (middle layer): involuntary smooth muscle that expands and contracts

blocks.html:
Atherogenesis: the process of atherosclerotic plaque formation
  • Exaggerated repair process (long-term, low-grade inflammation)
  • Players: platelets, macrophages, endothelium, smooth muscle

cells, extracellular matrix, lipids, growth factors, cytokines

1.Chronic endothelial injury: hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, homocysteine,

hemodynamic factors, toxins, viruses, immune reactions

2.Endothelial dysfunction (increased permeability, leukocyte adhesion); monocyte and platelet

adhesion and emigration

3.Smooth muscle emigration from media to intima; macrophage/histiocyte activation

Fatty streaks – precursor lesion of an atherosclerotic plaque

4.Macrophages and smooth muscle cells engulf lipid (cholesterol derived from the blood)

5.Smooth muscle proliferation, collagen, and other ECM deposition, extracellular lipid

Fatty streaks (aorta)

Raised plaques

Foamy macrophages/histiocytes; cholesterol clefts

blocks.html:
Coronary Artery Disease

Coronary artery disease (CAD)/ischemic heart disease: a group of cardiovascular diseases that are characterized by reduced blood

supply to the heart – angina, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, sudden cardiac death

The incidence of death by heart disease hasdecreased due to decreased smoking, importance of exercise, and pharmacological

  • management (statins, antiplatelet agents); still remains a common cause of mortality

blocks.alt: Figure from the Coronary Artery Disease: Myocardial Infarction and Complications of Acute MI notes

blocks.html:
• Canada compares fairly well compared to other countries with regards to mortality in heart disease
  • Every 26 seconds someone will have an event; every 60 seconds someone will die from it
  • 1/5 deaths will be from atherosclerotic disease; 37% of those that have an event will die within a year

blocks.alt: Figure from the Coronary Artery Disease: Myocardial Infarction and Complications of Acute MI notes

blocks.html:
• Epicardial coronary arteries: run along the outer surface of the heart on the epicardium – R/L coronary arteries
  • Subendocardial zone: furthest from the blood supply; suffers first when circulation is compromised
  • The arrangement of coronary circulation varies

Overlap of vascular territories/supply due to development of collateral vessels and anastomoses – can tolerate a

  • o reduction or blockage without suffering tissue damage

Coronary artery dominance: defined by the vessel which gives rise to the posterior descending artery, which supplies

  • o the myocardium of posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum – R coronary artery (85%), L circumflex artery (15%)
  • Vessels initially expand to accommodate plaque growth (compensatory enlargement), but eventually become stenosed
  • No symptoms until late in plaque formation – angina patients usually have > 70% narrowing
  • Disease is often located in the proximal portions of medium and large sized arteries – reachable by surgery or catheters
  • Atheroma can be very focal along a coronary artery – rate limiting step for flow; local restoration of normal flow with surgery
  • Many patients have severe disease in multiple vessels, which makes treatment much more challenging
  • Investigation of angina: treadmill stress testing (ECG), coronary angiography (contrast dye)

Pathological Ax: percent reduction of cross-sectional lumen area compared to the normal vessel

  • o Angiographic Ax: percent of narrowing compared to the least stenosed area
  • o Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease
Coronary angioplasty and stenting
  • Catheter with a deflated balloon and deployable stent around it is inserted into the vessel and guided to the blocked artery
  • The balloon is inflated and expands the stent, which pushes the plaque against the sides of the artery and holds the vessel open
  • Plaques are intentionally ruptured and expanded by angioplasty, and may even dissect the vessel wall
  • Patients are anticoagulated to prevent thrombosis
  • Previously angioplastied and stented vessels can develop re-stenosis

Drug-coated stents are designed to reduce inflammation and slow re-stenosis
